title: Chapter 12
paragraphs: The young Princess Kitty Shtcherbatskaya was eighteen. It was the first winter she had been out in the world. Her success in society had been greater than that of either of her older sisters, and greater even than her mother had anticipated. To say nothing of the fact that nearly all the young men dancing at the Moscow balls were in love with Kitty, two serious suitors had already presented themselves this first winter: Levin, and, right after his departure, Count Vronsky.

Levin's appearance at the beginning of the winter, his frequent visits, and his obvious love for Kitty had led to the first serious discussions between Kitty's parents about her future, and to disputes between them. The prince was on Levin's side; he said he wanted nothing better for Kitty. The princess, for her part, going around the question in the way peculiar to women, maintained that Kitty was too young, that Levin had done nothing to prove his intentions were serious, that Kitty felt no great attraction to him, and other side issues; but she did not state the main point, which was that she was looking for a better match for her daughter, and that Levin was not to her taste and she did not understand him. When Levin had abruptly left, the princess was delighted and said to her husband triumphantly, "You see, I was right." When Vronsky appeared on the scene, she was even more delighted, confirmed in her view that Kitty was going to make not merely a good match but a brilliant one.

In the mother's eyes there could be no comparison between Vronsky and Levin. She disliked Levin's strange and uncompromising opinions, and his awkwardness in society, which she put down to his pride and his queer life — as she thought of it — buried in cattle and peasants. She had not at all cared for the fact that he, who was in love with her daughter, had kept coming to the house for six weeks as though he were waiting for something, looking it over, as if afraid he might do them too great an honor by making an offer, and failing to see that a man who keeps visiting a house where there is a young unmarried girl is bound to make his intentions clear. And then suddenly, without doing so, he had disappeared. "It's just as well he isn't attractive enough for Kitty to have fallen in love with him," the mother thought.

Vronsky satisfied every one of the mother's wishes. Very wealthy, clever, of aristocratic family, on the high road to a brilliant career in the army and at court, and a fascinating man. Nothing better could be asked for.

Vronsky openly flirted with Kitty at balls, danced with her, and was constantly at the house, so there could be no doubt about how serious his intentions were. But despite this, the mother had spent the whole winter in a state of dreadful anxiety and agitation.

Princess Shtcherbatskaya herself had been married thirty years ago — an aunt of hers had arranged the match. Her husband, about whom everything was well known beforehand, had come, looked at his future bride, and been looked at himself. The matchmaking aunt had ascertained and conveyed their mutual impression. The impression had been favorable. Afterwards, on a day fixed in advance, the expected offer had been made to her parents, and accepted. Everything had gone very simply and easily. So it had seemed to the princess at least. But over her own daughters she had felt how far from simple and easy was this apparently everyday business of marrying them off. The scares she had been through, the thoughts that had been brooded over, the money that had been wasted, the arguments she had had with her husband over marrying off the two elder girls, Darya and Natalia! Now, ever since the youngest had come out, she was going through the same terrors, the same doubts, and even fiercer quarrels with her husband than she had had over the elder girls. The old prince, like all fathers, was extremely scrupulous about the honor and reputation of his daughters. He was unreasonably jealous over his daughters, especially over Kitty, who was his favorite. At every turn he had scenes with the princess for compromising her daughter. The princess had grown used to this from her older daughters, but now she felt there was more reason for the prince's touchiness. She saw that in recent years much had changed in the manners of society and that a mother's duties had grown more difficult still. She saw that girls Kitty's age formed some kind of clubs, went to some kind of lectures, mixed freely with men, drove about the streets on their own, many of them did not curtsey, and — most importantly of all — every one of them was firmly convinced that choosing her husband was her own affair, not her parents'. "Marriages aren't made nowadays the way they used to be," was thought and said by all these young girls and even by their elders. But how marriages were made now, the princess could not learn from anyone. The French fashion — parents arranging their children's future — was not accepted; it was condemned. The English fashion of complete independence for girls was also not accepted, and was impossible in Russian society. The Russian fashion of matchmaking through go-betweens was for some reason considered unseemly; it was ridiculed by everyone, including the princess herself. But how girls were to be married, and how parents were to marry them off, nobody knew. Everyone with whom the princess had discussed the matter said the same thing: "For mercy's sake, it's high time in our day to throw out all that old-fashioned business. It's the young people who have to get married, not their parents, so we ought to leave the young people to arrange things as they please." It was easy enough for someone without daughters to say so, but the princess realized that in the process of getting to know each other her daughter might fall in love — and fall in love with someone who did not care to marry her, or who was completely unfit to be her husband. And however much she was told that in our times young people ought to arrange their own lives, she could not bring herself to believe it, just as she could not have believed that, in any age, the most suitable plaything for a five-year-old was a loaded pistol. So the princess was more uneasy over Kitty than she had been over her older sisters.

Now her fear was that Vronsky might confine himself to merely flirting with her daughter. She could see that her daughter was in love with him, and tried to comfort herself with the thought that he was an honorable man and would not do such a thing. But at the same time she knew how easy it is, with the loose manners of today, to turn a girl's head, and how lightly men in general regard that kind of offense. The week before, Kitty had told her mother about a conversation she had had with Vronsky during a mazurka. The conversation had partly reassured the princess; but completely at ease she could not be. Vronsky had told Kitty that both he and his brother were so used to obeying their mother that they never made up their minds to anything important without consulting her. "And just now I am impatiently waiting for my mother's arrival from Petersburg as something particularly fortunate," he had told her.

Kitty had repeated this without attaching any significance to it. But her mother had seen it differently. She knew that the old lady was expected any day now, that she would be pleased at her son's choice, and she found it strange that he should not make his offer for fear of vexing his mother. Still, she was so anxious to see the marriage made, and even more so to be free of her fears, that she chose to believe it. Bitter as it was for the princess to see the unhappiness of her eldest daughter, Dolly, on the point of leaving her husband, her anxiety over the resolution of her youngest daughter's fate absorbed all her feelings. Today, with Levin's reappearance, a fresh source of worry had opened up. She was afraid her daughter — who at one time, she had imagined, had a feeling for Levin — might, out of an excessive sense of honor, refuse Vronsky, and that Levin's arrival might generally complicate and delay the matter that had been so close to being settled.
"Now — has he been here long?" the princess asked about Levin as they returned home.
"There's one thing I want to say..." the princess began, and from her serious, watchful face Kitty guessed what was coming.
"Mamma," she said, flushing hotly and turning quickly to her, "please, please don't say anything about that. I know — I know all about it."
She wanted the same thing her mother wanted, but the reasons behind her mother's wishes wounded her.
"I only want to say that to raise hopes..."
"Mamma, darling, for goodness' sake, don't talk about it. It's so horrible to talk about it."
"All right, I won't," her mother said, seeing the tears in her daughter's eyes; "but one thing, my love — you promised me you'd keep no secrets from me. You won't, will you?"

"Never, mamma, no secrets," answered Kitty, flushing slightly and looking her mother straight in the face. "But there's nothing for me to tell you, and I... I... even if I wanted to, I wouldn't know what to say or how... I don't know..."

"No, she could not tell a lie with those eyes," the mother thought, smiling at her agitation and her happiness. The princess smiled to see that what was going on in her soul at that moment seemed to the poor child so enormous and so important.
